questions.stem: Which of the following is a liability?
questions.explanation: A liability is an obligation to pay an outsider. Supplier dues are a liability; cash, inventory and machinery are assets.

whyOthersWrong.why: Cash is an asset the business owns.
Inventory is an asset that will bring future benefit.
Machinery is a non-current asset.

questions.hint: Ask: does the business owe this to someone?

questions.stem: Capital contributed by the owner increases which side of the accounting equation?
questions.explanation: Capital is the owner's claim. Introducing capital increases the Capital element of Assets = Liabilities + Capital (and typically assets too).

whyOthersWrong.why: Cash does increase, but capital is the element directly credited.
Capital is not owed to outsiders.
Capital is not an expense.

questions.hint: Who does the business owe the capital to?

questions.stem: Assets are ₹6,00,000 and liabilities are ₹2,50,000. What is the capital (in ₹)?
questions.explanation: Capital = Assets - Liabilities = 6,00,000 - 2,50,000 = 3,50,000.

questions.stem: The going concern concept assumes the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future.
questions.explanation: Going concern is the assumption that the business will continue long enough to use its assets and settle its liabilities in the normal course.

whyOthersWrong.why: The statement correctly defines going concern.

questions.stem: Which of the following is recorded as a DEBIT?
questions.explanation: Expenses increase on the debit side. Capital, liabilities and income increase on the credit side.

whyOthersWrong.why: Capital increases are credits.
Liabilities increase on the credit side.
Income increases are credits.

questions.hint: DEAD = Drawings, Expenses, Assets, Decreases in liabilities.

questions.stem: Goods are purchased for cash. What is the correct entry?
questions.explanation: Purchases (expense) increase → debit; cash (asset) decreases → credit.

whyOthersWrong.why: Cash goes out, so it is credited, not debited.
No sale has occurred.
No sale has occurred; the payment is in cash.

questions.stem: Which account normally has a CREDIT balance?
questions.explanation: Income accounts increase on the credit side, so Sales normally has a credit balance. Assets and expenses have debit balances.

whyOthersWrong.why: Cash is an asset — debit balance.
Machinery is an asset — debit balance.
Rent is an expense — debit balance.

questions.stem: A decrease in a liability is recorded as a debit.
questions.explanation: Liabilities increase on the credit side, so decreases are debits.

whyOthersWrong.why: Only increases in liabilities are credits.

questions.stem: Capital of ₹1,00,000 is introduced in cash. The journal entry is:
questions.explanation: Cash (asset) increases → debit; Capital (owner's claim) increases → credit.

whyOthersWrong.why: Capital increasing is a credit, not a debit.
No bank account is involved.
Both the sides and the accounts are wrong.

questions.stem: Rent of ₹15,000 is paid by cheque. What is the entry?
questions.explanation: Rent (expense) increases → debit; payment by cheque reduces the bank account → credit bank.

whyOthersWrong.why: Bank goes down, so it is credited.
Payment was by cheque — bank, not cash.
That describes receiving rent in cash.

questions.stem: Goods are sold on credit to a customer. The entry:
questions.explanation: The customer (receiver of goods) is debited; Sales (income) is credited. Cash moves only when payment arrives.

whyOthersWrong.why: No cash moved in a credit sale.
That reverses the entry and misstates income.
This is a cash sale, not a credit sale.

questions.stem: A journal entry must have equal total ______ and total credits.
questions.explanation: Double entry requires total debits to equal total credits in every journal entry.

questions.stem: An account's debit side totals ₹50,000 and credit side ₹35,000. The balance is:
questions.explanation: Debits (50,000) exceed credits (35,000) by 15,000, so the balance is a debit of ₹15,000.

whyOthersWrong.why: The balance sits on the larger side — debit.
That is the total of both sides, not the balance.
Both the side and the amount are wrong.

questions.stem: An asset account normally has a credit balance.
questions.explanation: Assets increase with debits, so asset accounts normally show debit balances.

whyOthersWrong.why: Assets are debited when they increase.

questions.stem: A trial balance has debits of ₹1,20,000 and credits of ₹95,000. What is the missing balancing credit figure (in ₹)?
A balanced trial balance does NOT detect:

options.text: Posting a sale to the purchases account

questions.explanation: Errors that keep debits equal to credits — wrong account, full omission, or equal-sided wrong amounts — are invisible to the trial balance.

whyOthersWrong.why: A wrong-account error still balances.
A fully omitted entry removes equal debits and credits.
Equal-sided wrong amounts still balance.

questions.hint: Which errors leave debits equal to credits?

questions.stem: Where do trade payables (creditors) appear in the balance sheet?
questions.explanation: Trade payables are amounts the business owes to suppliers, expected to be settled within the operating cycle — current liabilities.

whyOthersWrong.why: Assets are what the business owns.
Payables are short-term obligations.
Capital is the owner's claim.

questions.stem: Sales ₹4,00,000; opening stock ₹40,000; purchases ₹2,40,000; closing stock ₹60,000. What is the gross profit (in ₹)?
questions.hint: COGS = opening stock + purchases - closing stock.

questions.stem: Insurance of ₹12,000 was paid; ₹3,000 covers next year. How is it treated?

options.text: P&L ₹9,000; prepaid insurance ₹3,000 as an asset
P&L ₹9,000; prepaid insurance ₹3,000 as a liability

questions.explanation: Only ₹9,000 belongs to this year. The ₹3,000 prepayment is carried forward as a current asset.

whyOthersWrong.why: The prepaid portion must not hit this year's P&L.
A prepayment is an asset, not a liability.
The full amount is not this year's expense.

questions.stem: Equipment costs ₹1,00,000, residual value ₹10,000, life 5 years. Straight-line depreciation per year is:

whyOthersWrong.why: That ignores the residual value.
That adds rather than subtracts residual value.
That is just the residual value.

questions.stem: Which pair is part of the golden rules of debit and credit?

options.text: Debit the giver, credit the receiver
Debit what comes in, credit what goes out
Debit all incomes, credit all expenses

questions.explanation: For real accounts: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. The other pairings are reversed or wrong.

whyOthersWrong.why: It is the receiver who is debited and the giver who is credited.
Expenses are debited and incomes credited.
Assets are debited when they increase; liabilities credited.

questions.stem: Under GST, output GST on a sale is:
questions.explanation: Output GST is collected from customers and remitted to the government, so it is a liability until paid. Sales are recorded net of GST.

whyOthersWrong.why: Input GST is the receivable; output GST is payable.
GST collected is not a cost to the business.
Sales are recorded net of GST.

questions.stem: Output GST collected is ₹30,000 and input GST paid is ₹18,000. What GST is payable to the government (in ₹)?
questions.hint: Set off input GST against output GST.

questions.stem: In consolidated financial statements, which is eliminated?
questions.explanation: Consolidation eliminates intra-group balances, transactions and unrealised profits so the group is reported as a single economic entity.

whyOthersWrong.why: External sales remain in the consolidated statements.
External payables remain.
External borrowings remain.

questions.stem: Unrealised profit on inventory sold by a parent to its subsidiary is eliminated in consolidation because:

options.text: Profit is only recognised when the inventory is sold outside the group
The parent cannot earn from its subsidiary

questions.explanation: Within a group, a transfer is not an arm's-length sale. Profit on inventory still held inside the group is unrealised and eliminated until the goods leave the group.

whyOthersWrong.why: The goods were physically transferred, but the profit is unrealised.
The subsidiary's profit is irrelevant to this adjustment.
The group can earn from transfers, but the profit is deferred.
